This appraisal is insufficiently anchored in the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Leilani, a 66-year-old curriculum designer, carried the weight of a past conflict that felt both profoundly real and disturbingly distant. Decades ago, as a young woman on a humanitarian mission in a volatile region, her life irrevocably shifted. She remembered the day vividly, yet also in fragmented pieces that refused to cohere into a full narrative. They had been transporting medical supplies when their convoy was ambushed. The air filled with the deafening roar of rotor blades as a military helicopter descended, its powerful downdraft whipping dust and debris into a blinding storm. Armed figures emerged from the chaos, their faces obscured, their authority absolute. Leilani found herself pushed, shoved, and held captive, utterly powerless as she watched events unfold around her, unable to intervene or even fully comprehend. The memory itself, she often thought, was so extreme it was hard to believe it actually happened to her. She knew what had transpired, but found herself unable to find words to describe it, the horror locked away behind a language barrier of her own making.

In the years that followed, the world outside her home in suburban America became a landscape of potential threats. The sound of a helicopter or any aircraft, even a distant one, could instantly transport her back to that dusty, terrifying moment, the intrusive memory coming to mind suddenly, chilling her to the bone. It was not just the noise; being in a situation where someone had power over her, even in benign contexts like a customer service interaction or a bureaucratic process, would trigger a profound unease, a familiar dread of losing control.

To cope, Leilani gradually built a life designed for maximum safety and minimal exposure. As a curriculum designer, her work was largely remote, allowing her to avoid going out for extended periods. She could work from her quiet home office, meticulously crafting educational materials, a task that offered a sense of order and control missing from other areas of her life. When she absolutely had to venture out—for groceries, or a rare appointment—she made sure to stay close to an exit, mentally mapping escape routes in any room she entered, a habit that had become second nature. Over time, she had also learned to steel herself against any strong emotion, fearing that allowing herself to feel any strong emotion would open a floodgate she could never close. Joy, sadness, anger—all were carefully modulated, kept at arm’s length.

This careful self-management, however, came at a cost. Leilani, now divorced, found herself feeling increasingly isolated and set apart from others. Casual conversations felt superficial, her inability to articulate the core of her trauma creating an unspoken barrier. She second-guessed her judgments constantly, often thinking, "I can't trust that I will do the right thing," a self-doubt that stemmed from the profound helplessness she experienced so long ago. This pervasive feeling of needing to be on guard all the time meant she rarely truly relaxed, her senses constantly scanning for potential threats, even in the safety of her own home. The quiet hum of the refrigerator, a neighbour's dog barking, the distant sirens—each sound was filtered through a lens of hypervigilance, demanding an assessment of its danger.

In recent months, the quiet hum of her carefully constructed life had begun to feel less like a sanctuary and more like a cage. Her work, once a source of comfort, now sometimes felt like another form of avoidance, preventing her from engaging with the world beyond her screen. The loneliness of her isolation had become particularly acute after a distant relative's passing, an event that highlighted how few genuine connections she maintained. She realized she was tired of living in constant readiness, tired of the fragmented echoes of a past she couldn't fully grasp or articulate, yet which dictated so much of her present. What frightened her most was the thought of facing the rest of her life this way, always on the periphery, always on guard, and always, fundamentally, alone. This realization, a quiet but persistent ache, was what finally prompted her to seek help.
